words: The hotel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they run our store out and everything. See, we had a beautiful store. Now we don't even have a store. We have to go to St. Mary's for our groceries.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And you see, we can't build anything yet because we don't have water and sewer. That's why we're working. See, we formed an association at first. Well, you can't get any EPA money from an association. It has to be a taxing body. And a water and sewer district is. So that's what you did. You made it into a district. But it took us all these years to do it because we couldn't get enough money. People donated money and we put on beer bus and other kind of parties to raise the money because everything was by donation and then I kept hounding the county commissioners and finally, a little less than a year ago, we finally got $1,200 out of the commissioners and we're able to form our district. Because the railroad, with all they owned here, they only gave us $100 towards helping us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that a donation? Everybody donates.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They weren't taxed or what? Well, they should have given us a couple thousand because that's why they moved the terminal out is on top of the water and sewer. They said it would take $2 million to put the water and sewer in here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This is really interesting, but I want to get some more information about you. I almost hate to ask, are you in any other clubs, groups, or societies? Oh yeah. I belong to a beach club

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and I belong to the Milwaukee Women's Club. It's a railroad club and I'm public relations for them. We used to have a real active sportsman's club and I was secretary of that. Assistant editor of a paper we put out, but that was back in the 30s and 40s. And the 50s. And then... Let's see, what else? I can't remember.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. Yeah, actually I would be more interested in the ones you're in now. But what's this book now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's just the community...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does this have what... Are you in it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I was...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now this was Community Leaders of America. I guess so. I guess if you couldn't become a community leader here, nobody in Avery could. And that was 1958? 72. Oh, I don't know what I'm thinking. Well, we're on it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course they've been inviting me every year, but I just sit on it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What does it entail? They ask you to write down again what you've done and send it in here. Who nominates you? How do they get you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know and they wouldn't tell me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, you have to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I bet if it involves somebody... It probably has to do with the railroad, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You don't think so?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I kind of think it had something to do with the high-ups in the forestry. When I used to write for the paper, I gave them... They had the best... Avery and Red Eyes District had the best news coverage of any ranger's districts in Region 1. So I think the supervisor... I got a hunch that the former supervisor or maybe one of his...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that could be. I would think it would be somebody that had other contacts outside. What other... As long as we're on this too, what other honors or awards have you received?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you don't get thanked for these things. You just get them and keep your mouth shut and you get more bitching and you do thanks.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I heard the same thing down in Orofino from a woman.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You've got to have a skin as thick as an elephant's. But it don't bother me because the town...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You see those people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: See, my dad was on the school board. When I first came here, there were all eighth grades in a one-room schoolhouse up on the hill. Well, then they built an addition and they wanted... Then they had a two-room schoolhouse and then underneath, they had three high school kids and they hired a professor to teach them and they sat around on dirt floors, on apple boxes around the furnace. And they had a year, their first year of high school there. Well, then my dad got on the school board and they built this schoolhouse over here in 1922. My brother gave the dedication for it and my roots go so deep in Avery that... I just can't let go. So no matter how they hound me, it don't bother me because I'm interested in Avery. Just think, there's only about a hundred and... I'd say 25 to 50 people that live here. We have a resident pastor. We pay him $300 a month and we pay for the parish needs, which is $35.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, is this out of taxes or donations or what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, this is out of our own personal pockets. We tithe and we can provide the spiritual leadership in our community. And it's non-denominational, so Catholics and Jews and anyone that wants to come, we all worship the same Lord. And we're able to do this. And also, our scouts are very, very active.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Boy scouts? Girl scouts?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know when they had that world jamboree here? I forget how many years ago. That our boy, an Indian boy here, that was adopted by one of the Avery families, carried the lighted fire from Greece and lit off the jamboree.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, is that right? You mean the World's Fair?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, the world jamboree.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At Farragut. Huh. The world, didn't you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was down in the southwest, so I didn't know too much what was going on.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, see, Farragut, they fixed up for the first world jamboree of boy scouts

speaker: Speaker 1
words: from all over the world. Okay, I think I have heard of that, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because it had national and world coverage all the time. Well, one of our boys from Avery was the one that lit that. That's something for such a small town. And not only that, you should go into school and see all the ribbons that have been worn by our scouts.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, now, how about back to you, how about, have you ever been, say, are there any things from county fairs or any of your paintings, have you ever gotten any?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, but I've helped a couple of gals get started on a career of painting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you? Here in Avery, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, one of them lives in Potlatch. Did you teach them? Yeah, I had a group.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Ah, so that's another occupation, my gosh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had quite a...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In the meantime, let me ask you some other questions. Besides, now, the painting, you mentioned fishing. That's one of your hobbies? And do you still hunt?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, but I look in their eyes and...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You look at their eyes, that's just what my father said. That's why he never got into hunting. 1949. 1949. Oh, let's see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I got this woman here to help me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was in where? In Avery. In Avery, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was a class. They don't have that little gal that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, where are you? I can't... Right there. Oh! In there. Oh, my gosh. Let me ask, Julia, can you take pictures of magazines? Do you have to do it in a studio somewhere? Of magazine pictures?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's one with a cardboard. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can't hold it. Yeah. That's too bad. I'd like to have a copy of this.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Babe, lay down.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let me... I'll get back to that later. What other interests or hobbies would you say you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To help my daughter. See, a lot of the years when I... When everybody was making all this fabulous money during the war, even sweeping up factories and everything, my salary in the post office was less than $1,000 a year. Oh. For many years, for several years. So I used to... There was a lot of fishermen come in, and I used to repair their fish poles if they'd break.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Gosh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was set up to fix their repair fish poles.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was in the 40s, probably, huh? Yeah. Right off the bat, I've got a question I want to ask you. Do you think if... Now, let's see, you... Let me remember what happened here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You got married in 1927, and you're only married a year. Do you think if you would have stayed married that you would have had so many different occupations? That's really something. And it looks like you didn't just find one thing and go off in that direction. You've really had varied occupations. Was that mostly just out of necessity, or did you just like it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I love this. See, my daughter thinks I'm crazy because I live in Avery. She lives in Billings.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Billings, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, she thinks it's wonderful. And the only one of my relatives, my youngest grandson, he thinks his grandmother's just right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He's the one that's here, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he loves Avery like I do. And we're a long ways from the doctor and everything, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that St. Mary's? Is that... Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, remember the flood we had in 74? Yeah. The awful January flood? Well, I have allergies. And I've been taking some kind of medication that didn't agree with me. And on, I think it was the 14th of January, at the peak of the flood, when everything was all, the railroad was washed out, the roads were washed out and everything. They flew a great big Huey in and put it down up there. I would have died, and they flew me to St. Mary's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They came and got you and took you, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They had to do the forestry cooperate. We have an RN here in Avery. She's married to a forestry technician.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, well, that's great.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And she had given me three shots of adrenaline, and I was still all puffed out and choked.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My arms were all in my hands out like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just had a reaction to the medication?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You see, I get this, I land in the hospital two or three times a year. I was in there, well, just in June. I had the reaction right in the doctor's office. And just within 15, 20 minutes, I just puffed all up, and they rushed me over to the hospital. It just scared my grandson to death. But you see, she thinks I'm nuts because I live here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, now this...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I trust in the Lord, and everything's always coming out okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're really a perfect person to ask what do you think the advantages are of a rural area over an urban area of living?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's just something that I feel so sorry for all those people that have never known it, and those who do live here and don't appreciate it. The pure air and the beauty, the setting, the beauty of it. Well, it's just out of this world. You go out in the evenings...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I agree with that. This morning when we got up and it was so quiet.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the fishing is wonderful. You take a community, a small community like this that is more or less isolated, they become dependent and work as a group together. We have... Well, everybody rallies to the aid of everybody else. And you can see by... We have more... Now, Carter down here and Clarkia there, our other two school units, they can't even have a PTA because they find them on recess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We understood there was quite a lot of controversy about the school district. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I understand. Yeah, and they wiped out. We were going to have a secondary school down here where Seawolf's and OU stayed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right there at the property, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, right there on the other side of the garage. We'd expended $37,000 on that. We had bonded and received, and they'd voted in a half a million dollar bond. And this one man stopped it because it wouldn't be built in his town right in Calder.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think accounts for the fact that Avery can work together in Calder can't?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because we're more or less isolated, these people are, to the most part, transients.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who are here in Avery?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Here in Avery. Now, that's surprising.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A group of transients could get in and work and cooperate and have all these blessings. We're so busy on the calendar that it's hard to find a night when there isn't something going on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can imagine that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we have, to be frank with you, we have a class of educated people that live here. I hate to have them hear I said that, though, and feel badly about it, but this is true. You take your forestry personnel, those families, they seldom stay more than three to five years. They support, they're the greatest supporters of our church, they're the greatest supporters of our PTA, and the greatest supporters of everything that we have, our church, our PTA, our Milwaukee Women's Club, and everything else.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you feel that's because, I mean, the success of Avery has to do with the fact that you've got people that are educated people who came in and they're isolated when they get here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I say, well, look here, we're isolated, we want the best for our kids, we're going to get in and help. Now the PTA supports two things that are just real outstanding, and one is our Scouts, a very, very active group, and the other is kindergarten. Oh. We have, they have supported the kindergarten, and the woman that teaches it donates every hour of her time five days a week, and has for three or four years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now you bring up another point.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the Milwaukee Women's Club donates the room, the space to have it in.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What, now we're talking about a rural woman, what do you see as the, how do you compare the life of a rural woman and an urban woman? You've been to Missoula and Denver, do you think there's more or less opportunity for a woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: More in a rural area. Do you think so? Far more. There's far more because there's not the competition. You take, if I were in a city, I would never, because it even bothers me to get up and talk to a group, although I've learned to do it. I've had to learn to do it in order to accomplish the things I wanted to accomplish for Avery. And if they come here with an open mind, the things they can do is just tremendous. Now, our trouble right now, we have less railroad involvement, families of railroad people, because there are younger kids that have come from cities that live in Avery, they just can't stand it, they're bored to death, they can't wait until the weekend to get out. They don't attend anything, they want to get off to the city and shop and do this and do that. Just look what they're missing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, what would you tell a woman like that, a young woman who had come from a city and you knew and she knew she was going to be here for three or four years, how would you tell her, what advice would you give her?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would tell her to be a doer, to be a doer, and the satisfaction she'd get out of the accomplishments that this little town is able to do is such a great personal satisfaction, that it'd far outweigh anything that she could do off in some city, shopping in the windows and going to a show or something. Because, see, we have ladies' Bible study every Wednesday noon, it's a luncheon thing, and then we study for a couple hours afterwards, and then on Monday nights we have adult Bible class where the men and the women come, and it's about an hour and they just serve coffee and cookies, but it's made these men who, they are participating within the church, and they get up on the platform and are helped with, they open the, give the opening prayer, and do all. Now, these are fellas, mostly forestry men, who see the need in a town like this, where there's two bars and nothing else for their kids, where they participate and make this thing a family thing, with picnics and parties and this and that, and it's done wonders for the kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's really something that you find both the men and women involved in.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because they're not sitting in front of the TV every minute.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, yeah. Gee, I could go on.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now these little, there's a group of boys in the 7th and 8th in high school that are building a cabin.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they're just, now they've got their shapes, they're going to shingle the roof, I guess it's 12 by 8, and everybody that's seen it says it's just beautiful.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's really neat. You know, I was over in Seattle this summer, and they have classes at the university in building log cabins, and we were laughing about some of the funny things they were doing in there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But you know, the thing, I had the most wonderful childhood, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, let me ask you about that. How do you compare, well, you've got your grandson now, your daughter's not here, but how do you compare family life for you, and maybe you want to include your daughter, or else just your grandson?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When I go to my daughter's house, I'm going nuts.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you compare it with your family life when you were a child? I know there's a million differences, but...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, yeah, there is, because now kids, so many kids want to be entertained. And I was so busy as a kid that I had to hurry and get my chores done so I could do all the things I wanted to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think you managed to, did your daughter manage to keep busy when you were raising her? And how about your grandson? No, my daughter was a different... Has that been preserved?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I wasn't able to do that. I think part of it was that she lived with Mother and I, and there was lack of that father image in the home. And so when the CCs came to build these roads, why, she was just nuts about the CC project.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How old was she then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was in the eighth grade. First year of high, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she get married fairly young?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, she had a year in the University of Montana, and so she was, what was she, I think she was 19.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, she was 19.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She married a fellow that, she was dispatcher for the ranger station, and she met a young man from Billings that, he was already engaged when he got here, but he didn't stay in place long because she grabbed him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she was back from school for the summer or something when she met him? Yeah, she was back from school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And she said, she told me when she went to college, she says, Mom, I'm not going to learn. I'm going to find a husband.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She was really honest about it then, wasn't she?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She said, because she'd been raised all along with two women, she said, I'm going to get married and have six kids. She missed it by one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, isn't that strange? You're more atypical, you know. You probably, of the two of you, you're much less traditional than she is. Or I don't know what she's...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, that's what she wanted. Well, I never could find a guy that, every person that I ever got engaged to, they said, well, don't quit your job. Did they? Yeah. Three times, and I thought, got to thinking, well, I want to give up my freedom, work in the post office and have to come home and take care of their needs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, you're talking about giving up your freedom, your free time after work. Yeah. You didn't mean give up your work and stay home. No. Would you have done that? If you had met the right person that would have...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If I had met the right... yeah, I would have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: With all these jobs that you've had, it looks like you just, it would have been too confining for you to just be stuck in a home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I shouldn't say just be...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: See, my mother wasn't too well the last ten years of her life, so I was quite confined to watching out for her needs, although she was queen of the house. I never learned to cook until she passed away. Yeah. Because she was queen of the kitchen and the house, and I brought home the bread and butter, and she did the managing. A marvelous job. Very frugal. There were times when I'd sit down at the table and I'd say, well, hello, old friend.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You'd seen it before, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Quite a few times before.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you have had opportunities to get married again, but you just have decided you didn't need that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No way. I never found a fellow that I'd give up my freedom for, especially when mother's left. We had the most wonderful friendship. She was a very brilliant woman. Although she herself had only had a seventh grade education, she was a very avid reader, and when I was in the post office and working and didn't have time to read, a lot of the time she'd go through the daily spokesman review and mark it, say these are of interest.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had your one daughter when you were married. You apparently then didn't want any more children bad enough to get married to have them. You're satisfied with just the one? Let's see, you came from a family. Well, your mom just had two, didn't she? So there wasn't a real large family. If you don't mind my asking, and if you do, just tell me. We don't have to go over it, but what... How about childbirth and birth control? What kind of information? Did your mother talk to you about it or did you just learn as it happened?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, you know, the old German way was... hush hush, you know, these things were... I think it was something that they figured that a person shouldn't know until they got married, well then that was kind of it. You know what I mean? My mother didn't even tell me when I got to the age of... what do you call it when you start your period? I was on a camping trip with a whole bunch of people up there and of course I knew vaguely that kids don't, about it. But our river used to be about 10, 12 degrees colder than it is. Of course I was out fishing, you know, wading up in here. And of course I was just very... I was so chagrined there for all summer long because I got these cramps so bad because I had started and didn't know it. I was just too busy fishing. They had to bring me home, they had to get a horse and bring me home. I was all...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh no! Well, yeah, the thing we have to do is go back and pick up some of the other women. This always happens, you know, we get into the questions. There's much more I want to ask than we've got time for. Some of these we've already gone over. Well, let's see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, what you should do is send me your questionnaires.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, well, that's not fair. I'd rather listen.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was going on to tell you, my dad's the one that told me about the birds and the bees. Oh, is he? Yeah. Not my mother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, that's something. Yeah, that's unusual.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: After this happened to me, and gee, they had a nurse working on me for three days. I guess I was really sick.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because, you know, it was that river just like ice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, well, yeah, the first time I imagine you were just mortified to have that happen.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I was because of the war time. Some of the guys, you know, they'd look at you and grin, how are you feeling?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, oh, I can imagine.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I could just die. I could have fallen through the...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You might have thought about leaving Avery forever then, huh? What about your daughter? Did you, by the time she came along, did you tell her?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I told her, but she could have probably told me things. Because by that time, you know, it wasn't the moot question that used to be. People talked about it, you know, and it was discussed in school and everything. And this was good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How about when you had her, did you have her in a hospital or at home?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In a hospital.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In a hospital. How do you feel about the medical service you got? Did you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Real good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the doctors give you information or did they pretty much leave you in the dark and...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they... Well, I don't know because I haven't anything to compare it with now because I haven't asked my own daughter about it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How her experience was. Let's see, she was born in 28.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you... I think... Well, this town is still... We have, you know, young folks living together, which is a pattern in the city. We older generation, we don't like it, but we go along with it because we realize that's the new way of life. That's the new mode.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, you haven't remarried, but do you feel then that marriage is a... A worthwhile institution to save?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I really do, yeah. I really do for the children's sake. Now, we have a couple living up there in the canyon who are living together, Chris. She's got a little... What is he? Five, four-year-old boy? And it's just battered from pillar to post. Now, I have a granddaughter, my oldest granddaughter, who is a divorcee. Her husband ran off with another woman, and then she fell in love with this fella, and they lived together. Well, my little great-granddaughter, she was pulled from one to the other, to one, and she's real... She's too attached to her mother because her mother is the only one where she can find security.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A stable one, yeah. The one she's always got to go back to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, of course, I didn't like it, and I told my granddaughter I didn't. And she was just heartbroken because she thought that he would eventually marry her, but he didn't. So, where there's a child... No. Now, my oldest grandson is married, his wife, and divorced. They have... I have a great-grandson. And a great-granddaughter. And he married before he finished high school. And then they had a child, and then... Her folks interfered, and they split up. Mostly because my grandson hadn't grown up enough to hold a job more than three months. He pumped gas here and did this there, and something else there. Well, then he met this other girl in Missoula, and she was neat. And... He was off of marriage as an institution. But, after she lived with him, he was the one that wanted to get married to her. But they were married, and they were really happy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you... Now, you've got your daughter, and then...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, there's... That's two of mine. Well, now Rick and my second... My next grandson, Steve, they both saw what their older brothers and sister did. Well, they don't want any of that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They don't want any marriage or living together, or what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they don't. Not until they're stabilized.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, what do you see for those grandchildren? Do you think they'll...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: These two? Yeah. Yeah, well, I think that they'll both be stabilized and have a way of life before... They... And they'll look the field over before they get married. I really think...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you think they'll end up getting married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do think they'll get married, yeah. Of course, my youngest granddaughter is 13, so... I... I don't know idea how she feels. Whether she looks at that, but she knows the agony and the grief that... that the other two went through.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then if they look at you at all and ask you about it, they see there's another alternative, you know. Nobody can say you haven't had a full life. Oh, I have. My gosh, but that thing you've done. I guess... Actually, you've covered most of the questions without me having to ask them, which was really nice. I think one thing that is always kind of interesting to ask is... World War II and the Depression, did those... Did those have a very... Do you think they had a very big effect on your life? They were good for us. Do you think so?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. I wish... When I see the way my daughter throws one-third of what they buy to put on the table in the garbage.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you think they were strengthening...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think very much so, yeah. ...experiences. But you see now, this recession, this depression, it's different. We didn't have... What do you call it? Unemployment compensation. Now...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think that rural people, people that are used to... Well, I don't want to answer my own question. Do you think that rural people are more self-sufficient? Do you think they're better able to cope with economic hardships or hardships in general? I do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do because most of them, outside of Avery, of course now Avery is more and more being able to buy land from the railroad, that they have that plot, they can raise their own, they can provide for themselves. Where city people, you know, gosh, they're... I just think when the gas shortage comes this way, I feel so sorry for those people in these big cities where they... If we have a hard winter, god, that'll be terrible. It's just... And of course we can always go out and pick up a dead tree in Berlin. You know? Yeah. And we've got game. Well, this is just like being in heaven here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It is. It's really nice to hear somebody that's so pleased about where they are.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But this is what I don't understand about the community in Polder. How come... How is it, how come it is that they don't... I've studied and studied and studied and tried to figure out why is it that that group don't work together? Because some of them have lived there, they're grandfathers and they're...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think maybe that is the difference? You're talking about people coming in from the outside and saying, well, we're here, we might as well make it. Now those people, some of them have been there for a long time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's only the educated people that will do it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You think so?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's the people that have had one or two years of college...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that can see ahead, maybe.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And have been out in the world. And can see this. These people down there are provincial or something. They don't have any cash unless they sell a cow or something.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now the mill is a pretty big... The laundry yard, is that a pretty big employer down there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it is. But then it shuts down. Your economy is according to whether they're building houses or not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that's right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And this is bad because they have to depend on another source. No, I truly believe that education is just everything. Because these people have read enough and seen enough that even though they're coming in as trenches... Of course, you get the odd family that won't have anything to do with anything, you know. But that isn't the rule. And now we've got a new family just moving in up there on the hill. And I'll bet you within two or three months that woman will be so involved.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The woman. Now what about the man? Will he too? I mean, I know he'll have his job, but...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not always. Not always, but they're trained in the forestry area, I know. The public relations is a real part of their opportunity to be promoted on to another job. Now there's one man over there that... The family that moved out, he had to take a lateral, which means he didn't get a step up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, yeah. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because he and his wife wouldn't have anything to do with community, only with this little forestry clique. They weren't part of the whole set-up, so...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, well let me ask you... I don't know if you're even interested in it, but... What do you think when you hear about the women's movement? Or, you know, women saying, I'm not fulfilled, I'm not satisfied, I don't know who I am.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, almost everything in our country, it's good or overdoing it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, we heard that before, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Like these miners over here now. It's fine if women want to go in the mine.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was up at Kellogg, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, okay. But they should all... If she wants to be a miner, she better use the same pot. You see what I mean? I mean, I'd hate to see it come to the point, maybe I'm old-fashioned, where I'd be sitting on a pot here, and a man would be urinating right next to me. I mean, I just don't...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think there's... I think the woman loses something. I really do. I may be wrong. But I watch a lot of these women-lived things on TV and everything. And I think the idea is good, because I do think the women have been held down. We have a woman living up the street here whose husband has always been very jealous of her. And he lived here quite a while and had a big family. And it's only just now that he's mellowed to the point where she can hold offices and do it. She's a very brilliant woman. Very talented in many, many ways. Well, this is not right. You know, I mean... There's so many women like that that have so much to give. The pressures at home, and there's so much buying between husband and wife as to who's going to be the big shot. And it's too bad. So I can see, just like with our environmental protection, they went over backwards, they took it too far. I've been trying all summer long to get a permit for shakes. To shake my... Because it leaks. Well, I've lived here for over a half-century, and we've always been allowed to get anything that was fallen down, ready to rot, you know, to go and take it. Well, I couldn't get a permit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, is that right? Cedar?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Cedar, yeah. So now I finally got one. This man was going by the book. Just by the book, right down the line. There's got to be elasticity. Government bureaucracies, they're too powerful if they go by the book.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you say that goes for the women's movement, too, don't you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. I mean, it goes over... They go over backwards. Because, see, the women that are active in it, most of them, I imagine, are level-headed. But you take these emotional women, who go off on a tangent, you can take two or three of, say, 1,500 people, and you take those two or three, and that will ruin the whole movement. Because they just...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They get the publicity.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they get the publicity, and they go over backwards. Well, that's always what's written up, and this is bad. It's bad for the movement.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I got just one more thing to ask, and this is very general. Is there anything that you feel you'd like to say about who you are and how you feel about yourself and, you know, how you feel about the path that you've chosen? Are you happy with your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've been very blessed to... that my mother came to America, and I wasn't in Germany during World War II. And I was very blessed to be able to live in a town like this that has everything in it that a person would want. Not so much material things, because we weren't able to own our land, and you can see my furniture is all beaten up, but it don't bother me. It's livable. I live with it. I love it. You see? And I think it's an attitude within yourself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was just going to ask, I bet you could be put down in a lot of... could have said the same thing about it, I mean, because you would have made it as much a part of you as you did anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I just... I'm real pleased. I know where I'm going when I leave this old earth, because I have this strong faith. And this is real important, to use your peace. No matter what's going on in the world. I'm not a religious fanatic. I just read the Bible and I believe in it. And I know the Lord's coming back after us one of these days and rapture us out, and then there'll be a greater life on. So, you see, I have something to look forward to. Anytime anybody has a goal or something to look forward to...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that's what you're saying.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You can do most... you can put up with most anything. It doesn't terrify me if I have a allergy attack. Really. I mean, in this respect. Because I'm ready anytime. And my mother felt the same way, you know. You know, this was a wonderful blessing for me, because so often I've known so many other older people that they just grasp after their youth, you know. And without that spiritual knowledge and blessing, as they approach age and get older, it's awful to see them. They're terrified of death. They're terrified of their bones, arthritic bones getting worse.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, and they get very, very concerned with their body.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and they get so filled with themselves, they don't know what's going on in the world. But my mother wasn't like that. And this was real... This was real fortunate for me. Because I had the happiest last 20 years of her life. Gosh, we were happy. And she was so wise about world affairs and everything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think that's just the perfect place to end. I can't imagine anything...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can't imagine anything better.
